tip: No 'your' needed – Korean drops possessives when context is clear: 생일이 언제예요? (saengil-i eonje-yeyo?) is just 'when is birthday?', understood as yours.
Negation is the tiny word 안 (an) placed right before the verb: 안 먹어요 (an meogeoyo = not eating). No 'don't' verb needed.
'How do I get there?' has no 'get' or 'there' in Korean – 가다 (gada = go) does the work: 어떻게 가요? (eotteoke gayo?) is just 'how go?'.
일 (il) means work, day, and the number one – context decides. In 일이 어때요? (ir-i eottaeyo? = how is work?) it's your job.

english: I drink one cup of coffee.
tip: Count things with native numbers + a counter: 한 잔 (han jan = one cup), 두 명 (du myeong = two people).
The count comes after the thing counted: 사과 한 개 (sagwa han gae = apple, one item) – noun first, then number and counter, the reverse of 'one apple'.
몇 + counter asks 'how many': 몇 명이에요? (myeot myeong-ieyo? = how many people?)
'Have' is really 'exist': 동생이 두 명 있어요 (dongsaeng-i du myeong isseoyo) = 'two younger siblings exist'. Korean states existence, not ownership.
Money uses Sino-Korean numbers + 원: 오천 원이에요 (ocheon won-ieyo = it is 5,000 won).
Korean counts big money in units of 만 (man = 10,000): 만 원 (man won = 10,000 won).

english: I do not have money right now.
tip: 'Not have' is its own verb 없어요 (eopseoyo), never 안 있어요 (an isseoyo): 돈이 없어요 (don-i eopseoyo = there is no money).
Hours use native numbers + 시: 세 시 (se si = three o'clock), 한 시 (han si = one o'clock).
반 (ban) = half: 두 시 반 (du si ban = half past two).

english: I get up at six o'clock.
tip: 에 after a time means 'at': 여섯 시에 일어나요 (yeoseot si-e ireonayo = I get up at six).
시 (si) = o'clock, 시간 (sigan) = hours of duration: 한 시간 걸려요 (han sigan geollyeoyo) = 'it takes one hour', not one o'clock.
Before a noun, 'what' becomes 무슨 (museun = what kind of): 무슨 요일이에요? (museun yoirieyo? = what day is it?). Bare 뭐 (mwo) can't sit in front of a noun.
English juggles at/on/in for time; Korean uses 에 (e) for all of it: 월요일에 (woryoire = on Monday). One particle covers the whole set.
The present tense covers the near future: 내일 가요 (naeil gayo = I am going tomorrow).

english: I go to school in the morning.
tip: 에 (e) does two jobs in one sentence: time in 아침에 (achime = in the morning) and destination in 학교에 가요 (hakgyo-e gayo = go to school).

english: A friend comes to our house.
tip: 와요 (wayo) = motion toward the speaker, 가요 (gayo) = away. From your point of view a friend visiting you comes: 집에 와요 (jib-e wayo).

english: Tomorrow I go to the market.
tip: 내일 (naeil = tomorrow) takes no time particle – 시장에 (sijang-e) keeps its 에, but 오늘 (oneul), 내일, and 지금 (jigeum) never take 에.

english: I come to school in the morning.
tip: Say 와요 (wayo) only while you're at school — 오다 (oda) means coming to where the speaker is now.

english: I go to the office by bus.
tip: 로 = by (a means of transport): 버스로 가요 (beoseu-ro gayo = I go by bus).

english: I go to a café with a friend.
tip: 랑 = with (someone), friendly in speech: 친구랑 (chingu-rang = with a friend).

english: I work at the office on Mondays.
tip: Two particles split the work: 월요일에 (woryoire) marks when, 회사에서 (hoesa-eseo) marks where the action happens – 에서 (eseo) for doing, 에 (e) for time.

english: I study at the library on weekends.
tip: 에서 (eseo) marks where an action happens: 도서관에서 공부해요 (doseogwan-eseo gongbuhaeyo = I study at the library). Plain 에 (e) only marks going to or being at a place.
Noun + 해요 makes an action verb: 운동해요 (undonghaeyo = I exercise, lit. do exercise).
한테 = to (a person): 엄마한테 전화해요 (eomma-hante jeonhwahaeyo = I call mom).

english: I exercise together with a friend.
tip: 같이 (gachi = together) looks like it should read ga-ti, but the t softens to ch before that i – say gachi.
'Like' is 좋아해요 (joahaeyo) with 를 (reul): 커피를 좋아해요 (keopi-reul joahaeyo = I like coffee). 좋아요 (joayo) without 하 (ha) means 'is good' instead.
